t: Figure 1. Animation: development compared with every El Niño since 1950

t: Figure 1. Animation: sea surface temperature, 2026/2027 and past very strong events
s: Water warmer than 28 °C, normally confined to the western Pacific, now reaches farther east along the equator than in 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 or 1982/1983 at the same point in the year.
k: Water warmer than 28 °C, normally confined to the western Pacific, now reaches farther east along the equator than in 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 or 1982/1983 at the same point in the year. Sea Surface Temperature The warm water spreading east
x: Animated month-by-month sea surface temperature across the tropical Pacific (NOAA OISST, 0.25°), from January of each El Niño's first year to December of the next, for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998, 1982/1983 and the 1991–2020 normal, with the Niño 3.4 average for each. El Niño is defined by unusually warm water in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. As the warm water spreads east, the rising air and heavy rain that normally sit over the western Pacific move east with it, which shifts weather patterns around the world. t: Figure 4. Eastern Pacific or Central Pacific El Niño?
s: So far 2026/2027 is a clear Eastern Pacific El Niño, like 1997/1998 and 1982/1983: the warming is centred near South America, while the central Pacific is close to normal.
k: So far 2026/2027 is a clear Eastern Pacific El Niño, like 1997/1998 and 1982/1983: the warming is centred near South America, while the central Pacific is close to normal. Sea Surface Temperature Along the equator and by region
x: Two indices that separate warming near South America (Eastern Pacific type) from warming near the date line (Central Pacific type), for 2026/2027 and four past strong events, and every El Niño since 1950 at its peak. Orange shows warming near South America, blue warming near the date line. In the lower chart each dot is one El Niño at its peak: dots high and to the left warmed mostly in the east; dots below the dashed line warmed mostly in the central Pacific. El Niños centred near South America and those centred near the date line shift the atmosphere's heating to different places, so they affect rainfall and temperature around the world, including California, differently. The strongest past El Niños for California rainfall, 1982/1983 and 1997/1998, were Eastern Pacific events. NOAA ERSST v5 Niño 3 (5°S–5°N, 150°W–90°W) and Niño 4 (5°S–5°N, 160°E–150°W) anomalies from 1991–2020, combined as in Ren and Jin (2011): Eastern Pacific = Niño 3 − 0.4 × Niño 4, Central Pacific = Niño 4 − 0.4 × Niño 3 when both have the same sign; 3-month means. ERSST v5 (NOAA PSL) Relative Oceanic Niño Index (NOAA CPC)

t: Figure 1. Animation: the tropical Pacific in 3D
s: In a normal year the warm layer is thin near South America; in 2026/2027 it has thickened there, so the cold water that normally cools the eastern Pacific stays far below the surface.
k: In a normal year the warm layer is thin near South America; in 2026/2027 it has thickened there, so the cold water that normally cools the eastern Pacific stays far below the surface. Ocean Heat Below the Surface The warm layer in 3D
x: Rotating 3D view of the tropical Pacific in a normal year and in 2026/2027: the top surface is the temperature at 5 m and the lower surface the base of the warm layer (the 20 °C isotherm), from January 2026 to the latest month. Each block is the tropical Pacific seen from the south-east, with Asia at the far left and South America at the right. The coloured lower surface is the base of the warm layer: red where it lies deep, blue where it is close to the surface. The thin top sheet is the sea surface temperature. The trade winds normally hold the warm layer deep in the west and shallow in the east. When the winds weaken during El Niño, the warm layer flattens, so cold water no longer reaches the surface near South America and the eastern Pacific warms from below. NCEP GODAS ocean reanalysis, monthly temperature in 10 m levels to 205 m, via NOAA PSL; normal = 1991–2020 mean temperature. NCEP GODAS ocean reanalysis (NOAA PSL)

t: Figure 2. Interactive 3D: warm layer, temperature layers and hottest water

k: Switch to Hottest water and compare 2026/2027 with Normal: the body of water above 28 °C is far larger in 2026/2027 and reaches much farther east. Ocean Heat Below the Surface The warm layer in 3D

Seeing the warm layer, its temperature layers and the volume of the hottest water in three dimensions shows where that heat is, and how much more there is than usual. NCEP GODAS ocean reanalysis, monthly temperature to 205 m, via NOAA PSL; volumes over 5°S–5°N, 120°E–80°W; normal = 1991–2020 mean temperature. NCEP GODAS ocean reanalysis (NOAA PSL)

t: Figure 3. Warm water stored before each El Niño began
s: 2026/2027 began with more warm water stored along the equator than most El Niños, and the store has kept growing since, to more than any past El Niño at the same stage.
k: 2026/2027 began with more warm water stored along the equator than most El Niños, and the store has kept growing since, to more than any past El Niño at the same stage. Ocean Heat Below the Surface Warm water building up
x: NOAA PMEL's equatorial warm water volume in the six months before every El Niño since 1980 began, and month by month from 18 months before to 12 months after. Top: one bar per El Niño since 1980, showing how much more warm water than normal was stored in the six months before it began. Bottom: the same measure month by month, with every event lined up on the month it began (dashed line). Warm water normally drains away once an El Niño is under way. Warm water must build up along the equator before an El Niño can grow (the "recharge"), and El Niño then drains it toward higher latitudes (the "discharge"). A large store before and during an event provides the heat that sustains warming at the surface. NOAA PMEL warm water volume (above the 20 °C isotherm, 5°S–5°N, 120°E–80°W), monthly from 1980; anomalies from 1991–2020. Event start: the first month of each El Niño in NOAA CPC's RONI (+0.5 °C or more). Warm water volume index (NOAA PMEL) Relative Oceanic Niño Index (NOAA CPC)

t: Figure 4. Animation: warm water moving across the Pacific
s: More warm water is stored along the equator in 2026/2027 than at the same stage of 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 or 1982/1983.
k: More warm water is stored along the equator in 2026/2027 than at the same stage of 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 or 1982/1983. Ocean Heat Below the Surface Warm water building up
x: Animated maps of the depth of the 20 °C isotherm (the thickness of the warm upper layer) from January of each El Niño's first year to December of the next, for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998, 1982/1983 and the 1991–2020 normal, with the equatorial warm water volume (5°S–5°N) and its departure from normal. Each map shows how far below the surface the warm upper layer reaches (the depth of the 20 °C isotherm). Dark red means warm water extends deep; blue means the warm layer is thin. Watch the band between the dashed lines: during El Niño the red area spreads east along the equator. Warm water volume is one of the earliest signs of El Niño: it builds up along the equator in the months before an event and is drained away from the equator as the event peaks and fades. NCEP GODAS ocean reanalysis, monthly temperature to 205 m, via NOAA PSL; warm water volume as defined by NOAA PMEL (above 20 °C, 5°S–5°N, 120°E–80°W). NCEP GODAS ocean reanalysis (NOAA PSL)

k: The hottest water has grown the most: the volume warmer than 28 °C is far above normal and above 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 and 1982/1983 at the same stage. Ocean Heat Below the Surface Warm water building up

t: Figure 1. Westerly wind bursts along the equator (Hovmöller)
s: From June to September 2026 the wind over the central Pacific was more westerly than normal on almost every day, by 4.5 m/s on average: a larger weakening of the trade winds than in 1997 (3.8 m/s), 2015 (2.9 m/s) or 2023 (0.4 m/s) over the same months.
k: From June to September 2026 the wind over the central Pacific was more westerly than normal on almost every day, by 4.5 m/s on average: a larger weakening of the trade winds than in 1997 (3.8 m/s), 2015 (2.9 m/s) or 2023 (0.4 m/s) over the same months. Kelvin Waves & Sea Level The wind bursts
x: Daily surface wind along the equator compared with normal, from October of the year before each El Niño to January after its first year, for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016 and 1997/1998: red streaks are westerly wind bursts. Time runs down the page, one row per day, from October of the year before each El Niño; position runs left to right from the western Pacific to South America. Red streaks are westerly wind bursts: spells of wind blowing toward South America, against the usual trade winds. Each strong burst is followed by a Kelvin wave in the figures below. The trade winds normally pile warm water up in the western Pacific. Westerly wind bursts briefly reverse them, sending pulses of warm water east as Kelvin waves; repeated bursts, and the weakening of the trade winds as the ocean warms, are what turn a developing El Niño into a strong one. NOAA NCEI Blended Sea Winds v2, daily 10 m zonal wind (0.25°), averaged over 5°S–5°N; anomalies from the NCEI 1991–2020 monthly climatology; 5-day running means. Days missing from NCEI's record (all of May 2026) are filled with CCMP v2.1 near-real-time winds (Remote Sensing Systems), adjusted to match NCEI. Blended Sea Winds v2 (NOAA NCEI) CCMP v2.1 near-real-time winds (Remote Sensing Systems, via NOAA PIFSC ERDDAP)

s: A series of Kelvin waves has carried warm water from the western Pacific to South America since late 2025, each one adding to the warm layer in the east.
k: A series of Kelvin waves has carried warm water from the western Pacific to South America since late 2025, each one adding to the warm layer in the east. Kelvin Waves & Sea Level The Kelvin waves
x: Every Kelvin wave since October 2025 traced in daily satellite sea level along the equator: each pulse raises sea level by a few centimetres as it crosses the Pacific. Top: sea level height (SSH) along the equator on the day shown, rising in the east as warm water piles up. Bottom: the Kelvin-wave signal day by day, with time running down the page, so each wave is a red streak slanting down to the right. White dashed lines trace each wave once it has crossed the Pacific. Use the cm and inches buttons above the figure to switch units. Kelvin waves carry warm water from the western to the eastern Pacific. Each one deepens the warm layer in the east and warms the surface there one to two months later, which helps forecasters anticipate further warming. NOAA blended satellite altimetry, daily sea surface height anomaly (0.25°), averaged over 1°S–1°N, via NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP; anomalies from the 2017–2024 seasonal cycle. Blended satellite sea level (NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP)

t: Figure 3. How fast the Kelvin waves crossed the Pacific
s: The 2026 Kelvin waves were not unusually fast: they crossed at a median of 2.8 m/s, about 53 days from 150°E to 95°W, the same as the median of all clear waves since 2017.
k: The 2026 Kelvin waves were not unusually fast: they crossed at a median of 2.8 m/s, about 53 days from 150°E to 95°W, the same as the median of all clear waves since 2017. Kelvin Waves & Sea Level The Kelvin waves
x: The speed of every Kelvin wave traced in satellite sea level since 2017, and the days each took to cross from 150°E to 95°W, against the ENSO state at the time. Each dot is one Kelvin wave, placed at the date it was halfway across and at its speed; the right-hand axis gives the same speed as days to cross. Bigger dots raised sea level more; the bars show how precisely each speed is known. The grey band is the speed theory predicts for the fastest type of Kelvin wave; red and blue shading mark El Niño and La Niña. The speed of a Kelvin wave sets how long the warm water takes to reach South America, and so how much warning the ocean gives before the eastern Pacific warms. Speed depends on how the ocean is layered: a thicker warm layer and eastward currents make waves faster. NOAA blended near-real-time altimetry (sea surface height anomaly, 0.25°, daily, from 2017), 1°S–1°N, via NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP; ENSO state from NOAA CPC's RONI. Blended satellite sea level (NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP) Relative Oceanic Niño Index (NOAA CPC)

Load the view, then drag to rotate and use + and − to zoom; the angle you choose is kept while the days play. Sea level height (SSH) shows the full rise; Kelvin-wave signal removes the slow build-up so that the waves stand out as red ridges travelling from left to right along the equator. Satellite sea level gives a daily, ocean-wide picture of where El Niño's heat is accumulating and of the Kelvin waves that carry it east; higher sea level along the coasts of the Americas is itself one of El Niño's effects. NOAA blended satellite altimetry, daily sea surface height anomaly over 12°S–12°N at 1°, via NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP; anomalies from the 2017–2024 seasonal cycle; wave signal = anomaly minus its 91-day running mean. Blended satellite sea level (NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP)

k: By August 2026 coastal sea level had risen about 25 cm in Ecuador and 14 cm at San Diego, but not yet in Oregon and Washington; in 1997 the northern coast rose from the middle of the year. Kelvin Waves & Sea Level Along the coast from Ecuador to Washington
x: Daily tide-gauge sea level along the Pacific coast of the Americas, from Peru and Ecuador to Neah Bay, Washington, for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016 and 1997/1998. t: Figure 3. Global temperature and El Niño
s: Many of the record-warm years since 1950 coincided with El Niño, which temporarily adds to the long-term warming.
k: Many of the record-warm years since 1950 coincided with El Niño, which temporarily adds to the long-term warming. Records & Forecasts
x: Annual global mean surface temperature anomalies; recent record years have coincided with El Niño events.  El Niño releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere, temporarily raising global average temperature on top of long-term warming; the year during or after a strong El Niño is often a new record. NOAA NCEI global land and ocean surface temperature (NOAAGlobalTemp), relative to 1901–2000; El Niño winters from NOAA CPC RONI (December–February). Global temperature series (NOAA NCEI Climate at a Glance) Relative Oceanic Niño Index (NOAA CPC)

s: Summer 2026 nights were among the warmest on record across the region; daytime highs were less exceptional.
k: Summer 2026 nights were among the warmest on record across the region; daytime highs were less exceptional. Heat
x: June–September 2026 daytime-high and overnight-low anomalies across Southern California (NOAA nClimGrid, ~5 km), and the regional overnight-low anomaly for every summer since 1950.  El Niño's main influence on Southern California comes in winter. This summer's heat coincided with the developing event and record-warm coastal water, so these maps put summer 2026 in context. NOAA NCEI nClimGrid monthly (~5 km) mean daily maximum and minimum temperature, June–September, land only; anomalies from 1991–2020. nClimGrid monthly (NOAA NCEI)

t: Figure 2. Warm nights and hot days by station
s: Warm nights were far more frequent than usual in summer 2026 at every station, and Santa Barbara set a record.
k: Warm nights were far more frequent than usual in summer 2026 at every station, and Santa Barbara set a record. Heat
x: Station counts of warm nights (≥ 65 °F) and hot days (≥ 90 °F) each summer since 1950 at Los Angeles, San Diego, the Inland Empire and Santa Barbara.  Warm coastal water keeps nights warmer near the coast, and El Niño years can bring warm water to Southern California; the station records show how this summer compares with past El Niño and other years. NOAA NCEI GHCN-Daily station records (Los Angeles, San Diego, Inland Empire, Santa Barbara), June–September; El Niño strength from NOAA CPC RONI. GHCN-Daily stations (NOAA NCEI) Relative Oceanic Niño Index (NOAA CPC)

t: Figure 3. Marine heat in the Southern California Bight
s: Coastal waters off Southern California have had more marine heatwave days in 2026 than in any previous year by the same date.
k: Coastal waters off Southern California have had more marine heatwave days in 2026 than in any previous year by the same date. Heat
x: Daily sea surface temperature and marine heatwave days in the Southern California Bight since 1982 (NOAA OISST), with 2026 compared with 1997 and 2015. A marine heatwave day is part of a spell of at least five days when the water is warmer than 90% of past values for that time of year. Each year is compared through the same calendar date. El Niño can warm the waters off California, through ocean waves travelling up the coast and changes in the winds. Marine heatwaves affect fisheries, kelp forests and coastal temperatures. NOAA OISST v2.1 daily sea surface temperature (0.25°), via NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP, averaged over the Southern California Bight; marine heatwaves after Hobday et al. (2016). OISST v2.1 daily (NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP)

t: Figure 4. Animation: marine heatwaves from California to Peru
s: On 20 October 2026 the whole coastal ocean off Ecuador and Peru was in a marine heatwave, 70% of it Severe or Extreme, and half the coastal waters off Southern California and northern Baja were in a Strong or Severe heatwave.
k: On 20 October 2026 the whole coastal ocean off Ecuador and Peru was in a marine heatwave, 70% of it Severe or Extreme, and half the coastal waters off Southern California and northern Baja were in a Strong or Severe heatwave. Heat
x: Daily marine heatwave category (I Moderate to IV Extreme) across the eastern Pacific from 25°S to 45°N since January 2026 (NOAA OISST), with the share of the coastal waters off Southern California and off Ecuador and Peru in each category. Colours show the category of marine heatwave on each day: the more times the water exceeds its usual range for that time of year, the higher the category. Light grey-blue is ocean with no heatwave. The charts on the right show how much of each coastal box (A and B on the map) was in each category as the year went on. El Niño warms the coastal ocean of the Americas through coastal Kelvin waves and weaker winds. Prolonged marine heatwaves stress fisheries, kelp forests and coral, and can bring toxic algal blooms and unusual marine species to Southern California. NOAA OISST v2.1 daily sea surface temperature (0.25°, used every 1°), via NOAA PSL; marine heatwaves and categories after Hobday et al. (2016, 2018), with a 1991–2020 baseline. OISST v2.1 daily (NOAA PSL)

t: Figure 5. Long-term increase in summer heat
s: Summer nights across Southern California have warmed more than summer days since the mid-20th century.
k: Summer nights across Southern California have warmed more than summer days since the mid-20th century. Heat
x: Change in summer daytime highs and overnight lows since 1951–1980 across Southern California, and the regional summer temperature record since 1895 (NOAA nClimGrid). t: Figure 2. Precipitation in strong El Niño winters

k: El Niño
x: A periodic warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, with related changes in winds and rainfall, recurring every two to seven years.
s: A periodic warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, with related changes in winds and rainfall, recurring every two to seven years.

k: La Niña
x: The cool counterpart of El Niño: below-normal ocean temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.
s: The cool counterpart of El Niño: below-normal ocean temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.

k: ENSO
x: El Niño–Southern Oscillation: the cycle of El Niño, neutral and La Niña conditions and the related swing in air pressure across the tropical Pacific.
s: El Niño–Southern Oscillation: the cycle of El Niño, neutral and La Niña conditions and the related swing in air pressure across the tropical Pacific.

k: anomaly
x: The difference from normal (the 1991–2020 average) for the same time of year; +2 °C means 2 °C warmer than usual.
s: The difference from normal (the 1991–2020 average) for the same time of year; +2 °C means 2 °C warmer than usual.

k: Relative Oceanic Niño Index
x: NOAA's official El Niño index (RONI): the Niño 3.4 anomaly measured relative to the average of the whole tropical ocean, so that general warming is not counted as El Niño. Three-month averages.
s: NOAA's official El Niño index (RONI): the Niño 3.4 anomaly measured relative to the average of the whole tropical ocean, so that general warming is not counted as El Niño. Three-month averages.

k: RONI
x: Relative Oceanic Niño Index, NOAA's official El Niño index: the Niño 3.4 anomaly measured relative to the average of the whole tropical ocean. Three-month averages.
s: Relative Oceanic Niño Index, NOAA's official El Niño index: the Niño 3.4 anomaly measured relative to the average of the whole tropical ocean. Three-month averages.

k: Niño 3.4
x: A region of the central equatorial Pacific (5°S–5°N, 170°W–120°W) whose temperature is the main measure of El Niño.
s: A region of the central equatorial Pacific (5°S–5°N, 170°W–120°W) whose temperature is the main measure of El Niño.

k: Niño 1+2
x: The region off the coasts of Peru and Ecuador (10°S–0°, 90°W–80°W).
s: The region off the coasts of Peru and Ecuador (10°S–0°, 90°W–80°W).

k: Niño 3
x: The eastern equatorial Pacific, 5°S–5°N, 150°W–90°W.
s: The eastern equatorial Pacific, 5°S–5°N, 150°W–90°W.

k: Niño 4
x: The western-central equatorial Pacific, 5°S–5°N, 160°E–150°W.
s: The western-central equatorial Pacific, 5°S–5°N, 160°E–150°W.

k: thermocline
x: The layer where temperature drops quickly with depth, separating warm surface water from cold deep water; in the tropics it is marked by the 20 °C isotherm.
s: The layer where temperature drops quickly with depth, separating warm surface water from cold deep water; in the tropics it is marked by the 20 °C isotherm.

k: 20 °C isotherm
x: The depth at which the ocean is 20 °C, used to mark the base of the warm upper layer.
s: The depth at which the ocean is 20 °C, used to mark the base of the warm upper layer.

k: warm water volume
x: The volume of water warmer than 20 °C near the equator (5°S–5°N, 120°E–80°W). It builds up before an El Niño and is drained by it.
s: The volume of water warmer than 20 °C near the equator (5°S–5°N, 120°E–80°W). It builds up before an El Niño and is drained by it.

k: warm pool
x: The large area of very warm water (above about 28 °C) normally found in the western tropical Pacific.
s: The large area of very warm water (above about 28 °C) normally found in the western tropical Pacific.

k: upwelling
x: The rise of cold, deep water toward the surface, normally strong along the equator and off South America.
s: The rise of cold, deep water toward the surface, normally strong along the equator and off South America.

k: trade winds
x: Steady easterly winds over the tropical Pacific that push warm surface water toward the west.
s: Steady easterly winds over the tropical Pacific that push warm surface water toward the west.

k: Kelvin waves
x: Pulses of warm water that travel east along the equator beneath the surface, crossing the Pacific in about two months.
s: Pulses of warm water that travel east along the equator beneath the surface, crossing the Pacific in about two months.

k: Hovmöller
x: A diagram with position on one axis and time on the other, used to follow features as they move.
s: A diagram with position on one axis and time on the other, used to follow features as they move.

k: reanalysis
x: A best estimate of past ocean or weather conditions, made by combining observations with a numerical model.
s: A best estimate of past ocean or weather conditions, made by combining observations with a numerical model.

k: GODAS
x: NOAA's Global Ocean Data Assimilation System, an ocean reanalysis that estimates temperature below the surface.
s: NOAA's Global Ocean Data Assimilation System, an ocean reanalysis that estimates temperature below the surface.

k: OISST
x: NOAA's Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature: a daily 0.25° analysis of satellite, ship and buoy data since 1981.
s: NOAA's Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature: a daily 0.25° analysis of satellite, ship and buoy data since 1981.

k: ERSST
x: NOAA's Extended Reconstructed Sea Surface Temperature: a monthly 2° record since 1854.
s: NOAA's Extended Reconstructed Sea Surface Temperature: a monthly 2° record since 1854.

k: nClimGrid
x: NOAA's gridded (about 5 km) monthly temperature and precipitation for the United States since 1895.
s: NOAA's gridded (about 5 km) monthly temperature and precipitation for the United States since 1895.

k: GHCN-Daily
x: NOAA's Global Historical Climatology Network of daily weather-station records.
s: NOAA's Global Historical Climatology Network of daily weather-station records.

k: marine heatwave
x: A spell of at least five days when sea surface temperature is above the 90th percentile for the time of year (Hobday et al., 2016).
s: A spell of at least five days when sea surface temperature is above the 90th percentile for the time of year (Hobday et al., 2016).

k: water year
x: October to September, labelled by the year in which it ends.
s: October to September, labelled by the year in which it ends.

k: Santa Ana
x: Dry, often strong offshore winds that blow from the interior toward the Southern California coast, mainly in autumn and winter.
s: Dry, often strong offshore winds that blow from the interior toward the Southern California coast, mainly in autumn and winter.
